morningLine: The next adventure may arrive down the telephone line.

lead.headline: British Telecom prepares MUD 2: shared adventures by telephone
lead.dek: A commercial multiplayer adventure is planned for September, with forty lines to start.
body: British Telecom is preparing to turn the shared computer adventure into a commercial telephone service. Popular Computing Weekly reports on July 18 that MUD 2 is being developed for a planned unveiling at September’s Personal Computer World Show. This is a service in preparation, not a July opening.

Richard Bartle and Roy Trubshaw, creators of the original MUD at Essex University, are developing the expanded game commissioned by BT. The original adventure remains available at Essex and on Compunet. The new plan places a VAX 11/750 behind an initial forty telephone lines, with expansion beyond one hundred envisaged and play scheduled for evenings and weekends.

The proposed £20 MUD Pack includes registration, instructions, a map, a personal-code card and thirty credits of six minutes each. Further play is reported at £2 per hour, with telephone charges additional. A text adventure shared with other callers makes the cost of the connection part of the gaming decision.

The magazine specifies a 1275-baud modem and terminal-emulation software. If the venture succeeds, BT envisages putting the game on computers around the country. For now, the promise is a larger shared world beyond the standalone cassette: players will have to wait for the planned launch.

stories.headline: Sinclair puts its name on a floppy drive for the QL
body: Sinclair is to badge a Microperipherals 3.5-inch drive and interface for the QL, according to the July 18 front-page report. Availability is expected within a month. The move gives Sinclair’s name to a disk alternative while the company continues to support Microdrives.

The double-sided, double-density system provides 720 KB formatted capacity, or 1 MB unformatted. Its interface fits the QL expansion port, and up to four drives can be daisy-chained. No retail price is established in the report.

Microperipherals technical manager Richard Miller says the underlying drive has shipped since March and that Sinclair has considered badging it for about seven months. Miller wrote its DOS, which differs from the DOS on other QL disk units. This is a change of badge and policy rather than the invention of an entirely new drive.

stories.headline: Credit-card software takes aim at tapes and piracy
body: Astar International’s Sofcards package software in a thin plastic card with an edge connector. Electric Software of Cambridge is distributing the format in Britain. ROM or battery-backed RAM replaces the familiar cassette or disk, with a separate adapter required for each kind of computer.

MSX ROM games are already offered at £14.95 to £19.95. Adapters are expected to cost about £10; Spectrum and QL versions remain under development. Other proposed adapters must not be mistaken for products already on the shelf.

The companies promote resistance to copying, but price is the immediate obstacle. Electric Software’s Mike Hall says the games must reach £9.95 within a year for the scheme to succeed. Battery-backed timed licensing is discussed as a possible use, not as an established shipping system.

stories.headline: Amstrad 6128 may reach Britain this autumn
body: A British arrival for the disk-based 128K CPC6128 may come this autumn rather than next year, Popular Computing Weekly reports. The machine was shown to the American market at Chicago’s summer CES in early June; a British launch is still a reported possibility.

The proposed newcomer brings a revised keyboard, bank-switched 128K memory and enhanced CP/M and DR Logo compared with the CPC664. That makes the timing important for buyers considering a disk-equipped CPC today.

A September show appearance remains speculation. Infocom and Kuma express interest in supporting the machine, while Rumbelows is considering stocking it. Neither a confirmed retail agreement nor a verified British launch price is established by this report.

market.headline: New formats must earn their place beside the cassette
market.summary: Sofcards promise convenient loading but carry a price premium. Sinclair’s disk badge and Amstrad’s reported 128K plans give home-computer buyers more expansion choices, while BT tests the idea of paying for shared play by the hour.

worldAnchor.headline: Reagan doctors report cancer
worldAnchor.summary: On July 15, Dr. Steven Rosenberg announces that President Reagan has cancer, UPI reports. The medical announcement places this week’s computer news against a major national bulletin.

bbsNote.headline: MUD meets the telephone company; DataCOM doubles speed
bbsNote.summary: Two genuine dated beats: BT’s September multiplayer-game plans reported July 18, and July hobbyist reports of 2400-bps BBS upgrades. Posts below are editorial summaries, NOT fabricated historical message-board quotations.

posts.platform: BT planned MUD 2 / Essex MUD / Compunet
posts.text: BT commissions an expanded adventure from Bartle and Trubshaw; plans £20 registration pack and £2/hour plus telephone charges.
Steven L. Sanders reports 2400 support and US Robotics’s $350 active-sysop modem offer, expiring around July 15.
July newsletter announces a separate new-DOS-file area alongside CP/M files, showing mixed-platform user demand.

curiosity.headline: A software card that forgets when its battery dies
curiosity.summary: Electric Software discusses an unusual way to enforce a timed software license.
curiosity.detail: PCW July 18 p. 4 describes battery-backed Sofcards with estimated two-to-three-year battery life and discusses making business software depend on the card. The writer calls it self-destruction, but the mechanism described is loss of battery-backed memory, not physical damage. A proposed application, not verified commercial deployment.
